extracted.intended_audience: early-career and mid-career academic mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, assistant/associate professors)
extracted.subtask_short: tenure and career advice for mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines on getting tenure, being a productive/engaged tenured faculty member, promotion, teaching techniques, and career choices for mathematicians at a variety of institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure decision factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A tenure case is judged on three factors: (i) teaching, (ii) research, and (iii) service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three factors all count and a serious deficiency in any one can cost you tenure. Institutions weight them differently; they are not necessarily equal. Candidates should prepare a dossier addressing all three areas with concrete evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research expectations at major research universities
rubrics_metrics.description: At a research university the tenure dossier must demonstrate a major research program, typically supported by ten to twenty published papers and strong letters of recommendation (about six to ten) from outside experts, in a particular field of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers should be published in independent, peer-reviewed journals of good repute (Deans know the pecking order among journals). The dossier must make beyond doubt that you have an ongoing, significant research program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good external letter of recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good letter will be two to three pages long and very specific about the candidate’s attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such letters should include a reasonably detailed discussion of the candidate’s research and its significance, explicit binary comparisons with other young mathematicians at the same level, a description of teaching skills, and a discussion of professional activities (collaborations, talks, communication). The letter should make a very positive and explicit recommendation for tenure and leave nothing to the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching evidence required for tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching must be evaluated objectively and in detail in the tenure dossier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible evidence includes classroom observations with written reports, a precis of written student evaluations, polls of other faculty about the candidate’s teaching, and solicited letters from former students. The teaching section must be concrete and substantive—not vague praise or 'fluff'—so the Dean knows you will contribute to teaching for decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Service should be documented and taken seriously as part of the tenure case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document committee service at the Department and University level, undergraduate advising, Ph.D. supervision, and volunteer/professional activities. While service typically carries less weight than research or teaching, evidence of honorable and substantive service strengthens the dossier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional Tenure Document
rubrics_metrics.description: Most institutions have a Tenure Document describing what tenure means at that institution and the procedures for obtaining or losing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain and read the Tenure Document for your institution (it usually resides in the Chancellor’s/Dean’s office). It is a legal document that charts criteria, procedures, and expectations—know it well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution-specific weighting of evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Different institutions weight research, teaching, and service differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a front-line research institution may weight research ~75% with the remainder for teaching/service; a primarily teaching institution might weight teaching ~60% and service ~30% with research of lesser concern; some comprehensive schools may use other mixes (example given: teaching 50%, scholarship 25%, service 25%). Know your institution’s weighting and tailor your dossier accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: External versus in-house review practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for external letters and review vary by institution and department type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At top research universities external letters from prominent professors are standard. At many teaching schools tenure cases are decided primarily in-house (sometimes by filling out internal forms). Candidates have limited control over the process but may be invited to suggest letter writers or names to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate control and role in the tenure process
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidates have limited control over the tenure process and typically cannot steer it significantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may be asked to suggest names for letter-writers or to provide information about teaching/service, but mostly the department's processes (the 'spaghetti factory') take over. Prepare the best dossier you can and recognize you may receive few clues during the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing research problems (project sizing and strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose problems of the right size—ones you can make a dent in; be realistic about what a single person can accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid taking on problems so large they will swallow you (e.g., attempting to solve the Riemann Hypothesis alone). For very large projects, collaborate with trusted colleagues. Enter projects knowing precisely what you aim to accomplish; don’t go in blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinventing yourself and changing fields
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain a long and vigorous research life, consider changing fields every several years or taking on new projects every five years to stay fresh and engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing fields can prevent 'your field drying up' and help sustain enthusiasm. Take on new kinds of books, courses, responsibilities, or move communities to avoid rut and renewal of interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active-engagement teaching technique (Hald method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use in-class active practice: present two examples, have students do an example in class, check answers, then repeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique covers the same material but empowers students by confirming on the spot that they can do the work. Make it a ritual (e.g., hand out slips, assess how many got it right). The approach improves retention versus passive listening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for keeping teaching lively and connected
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate rapport and varied class devices to stay in touch with students and keep classes lively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contemporary touchstones (newspaper articles), vignettes and history of mathematics, amusing anecdotes about mathematicians, self-deprecating jokes, daily rituals, and non-exam mathematical snippets explicitly labeled as 'not on the exam' for cultural enrichment. Learn to speak in a way students understand; tailor language and examples to your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion to full professor considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotion timing and criteria vary: some institutions expect rapid promotion; others have fixed waits. Promotion relies on research, teaching, and service, and outside letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid being put up too soon (a failed case is demoralizing and delays the next opportunity). Chairs should consult Deans and gather outside letters; when letters or teaching/service/publication records are lacking, advise candidates to wait. Work with the Dean to strengthen borderline cases; alternative contributions (books, curricular leadership, outreach) can support promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons for tenure denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure denials often stem from interpersonal/teaching issues or insufficient research/other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include inability to get along with a senior mentor, poor teaching, or weak research output. Seek candid advice from mentors; heed counsel about readiness before going up for tenure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options if denied tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: If you do not get tenure, explore other academic jobs (often at lesser institutions) or careers in industry, research labs, or government agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many former tenure-denied mathematicians find satisfying careers in industry (software, finance), government (NSA, NASA), research labs, or start businesses (publishing, consulting, woodworking, etc.). Consider using a one-year lead time to find next steps if counseled to leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using tenure productively (post-tenure goals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure gives intellectual freedom and time to pursue big projects, effect departmental improvements, or take administrative roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the freedom to improve teaching quality, curriculum, collaborations across disciplines, or to attempt large collaborative research projects. Consider administrative service (Chair, Vice-Chair, rotating Dean) to make broader contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviving or redirecting a moribund career for promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: For faculty stagnating at Associate rank, alternative scholarly contributions can provide grounds for promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paths include writing an important book, creating outreach programs that attract students, leading undergraduate programs, or curricular/teaching initiatives. Chairs can work with individuals and Deans to strengthen cases where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-life balance and daily productivity targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage time by setting realistic daily goals and recognize when to stop for the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you do four or five hours of intense mathematical research daily plus a few hours of lighter related activity, you have likely done more than reasonably expected. Setting and meeting realistic goals lets you relax in the evening without guilt.
